newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian premier to visit Chechnya "in near future".
newsitem.headline: Russian premier to visit Chechnya "in near future".

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin is expected to visit breakaway Chechnya "in the near future" to step up the fragile peace process, Moscow's envoy to the rebel region said on Monday.
"The prime minister's participation in the negotiation process and in the solving of a whole series of urgent problems is becoming indispensible," Ivan Rybkin told the Ekho Moskvy radio station.
It would be Chernomyrdin's first known visit to Chechnya since fighting erupted when Moscow sent troops in December 1994 to try to halt the southern region's independence drive.

Rybkin, who did not say exactly when the visit would take place, met Chernomyrdin on Monday to brief him on his own talks with Chechen separatist leaders on Sunday in the Ingushetia region bordering Chechnya.

He said Chernomyrdin had approved the idea of setting up a free economic zone to help fund the post-war reconstruction of Chechnya. "Introducing special economic conditions is the best option for today," he told the radio.
Rybkin, who replaced the outspoken Alexander Lebed as Moscow's envoy to Chechnya one week ago, vowed to uphold a peace deal signed by Lebed on August 31.
He also gave a cautious welcome to separatists' plans to hold a regional presidential election in January.
"We were talking about elections on January 27. Why not? Why should I disagree?," he told Ekho Moskvy.
But he added that the elections should only go ahead if the region was completely demilitarised and the rebels laid down their arms -- something separatist leaders were unlikely to accept.

"All armed formations should lay down their arms. It should not happen that a person holding a grenade launcher in his left hand fills in a ballot paper with his right. This would be absurd," said Rybkin.
Until now Moscow had said little about the election plans, which have sidelined the Chechen government installed by Moscow at the start of the conflict and now virtually ignored.

Asked in his Monday radio interview who was now in control of Chechnya, Rybkin said: "For now we have the joint commission -- a sort of regional authority. When they elect a legislature and name a government, we will deal with this government."

The August pact, which ended 21 months of fighting which killed tens of thousands of people, involved a withdrawal of Russian troops from Chechnya and a pledge to defer a decision on the region's political status for five years.

But both sides have stuck firmly to their public positions on Chechnya's status, with Russia saying the region can never break away and the rebels repeating the independence declaration made by their late leader Dzhokhar Dudayev in 1991.
On the vexed issue of troop withdrawals, Rybkin signalled that he might be willing to compromise over two divisions that Moscow wants to leave in Chechnya despite rebels' objections.
"This issue can be the object of future negotiations," Itar-Tass news agency quoted him as saying on Monday.
